issues.legal_issue: A statutory definition of a paying guest that specifies its elements cannot be supplemented with additional requirements drawn from the law of lodgers or general notions of shared occupation and control.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether an occupier under the rent-control legislation was a paying guest or a licensee.
The legislation defined a paying guest by reference to the person not being a member of the licensor’s family, being given part of premises, and the licensor residing in those premises.
The lower courts relied on concepts of unity of residence and the licensor’s control or dominance, including principles associated with the English law of lodgers.
issues.conclusion: The statutory definition must be applied according to its stated elements; unity of residence, joint occupation, or the licensor’s control over the occupier’s part cannot be added as further requirements.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 5(6A), 5(4A) and 5(8) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a paying guest is a non-family member given part of premises in which the licensor resides; a paying guest is excluded from the definition of licensee, and premises include a part of a building. A definition beginning with “means” is ordinarily exhaustive and restrictive, so courts should not add elements absent ambiguity or compelling reason. The Court relied on Kishan Lal v. State of Rajasthan; P. Kasilingam v. P.S.G. College of Technology; Gough v. Gough; Punjab Land Development and Reclamation Corporation Ltd. v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court; and Inland Revenue Commissioner v. Joiner. It rejected importing the English-law attributes of a lodger, while referring to Surendra Kumar Jain v. Royce Pereira as consistent with the licensor residing in the premises without occupying the same room.

predicates.rent_control_definition_dispute: The proceeding concerns the classification of an occupier under rent-control legislation.
predicates.definition_states_specific_elements: The governing legislation defines the disputed status by specifying the elements that constitute it.

issues.definition: When a rent-control classification dispute turns on a definition that specifies its elements, the rule requires applying those stated elements without adding others.

issues.legal_issue: An occupier who is not a member of the licensor’s family and is given part of premises in which the licensor resides is a paying guest even if the occupier uses that part separately and exclusively, and is not a licensee who becomes a deemed tenant under the statutory conversion provision.
material_facts: The occupier was not related to or a member of the licensors’ family.
The occupier was given a bedroom, kitchen and bathroom within a larger terrace flat, while the licensors occupied the remaining portion of that flat.
The two portions were separate in use, but formed part of one premises with a common main entrance; the occupier’s portion was part of the larger premises in which the licensors resided.
The occupier sought recognition as a deemed tenant under the provision converting qualifying licensees in occupation of at least a room on the specified date into tenants.
The dispute reached the Court on appeal from a High Court ruling that the occupier was a paying guest.
issues.conclusion: The occupier was a paying guest, not a licensee entitled to deemed tenancy under section 15-A; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(6A), 5(4A) and 15-A of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provide that a paying guest is excluded from the statutory definition of licensee, while the deemed-tenancy provision applies to a qualifying licensee in occupation of premises or a part of them. The relevant requirements for paying-guest status are that the occupier is not a member of the family, is given part of the premises, and the licensor resides in those premises. Separate or exclusive use of the part does not prevent that classification where it remains part of the larger premises in which the licensor resides. The Court relied on its interpretation in Surendra Kumar Jain v. Royce Pereira and upheld the High Court’s application of the definition in Sarfarzali Nawabail Mirza v. Miss Maneck G. Burjorji.
